    What is EMDR therapy, and does it actually work?

    📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1689 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that clinically reviewed by Dr.
    • Maybe a friend swears EMDR helped her move past something she’d carried for years.
    • If you’re uncertain, that’s understandable, because EMDR can sound unconventional: you briefly recall a painful memory while following side-to-side stimulation, like tracking a moving target with your eyes.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

    Maybe a friend swears EMDR helped her move past something she’d carried for years. Or maybe you came across it online while searching for ways to cope with a memory that still feels heavy. Whether you’ve heard of EMDR but don’t know how it works, or you’re familiar with the approach but skeptical, we’re here to break it all down.

    If you’re uncertain, that’s understandable, because EMDR can sound unconventional: you briefly recall a painful memory while following side-to-side stimulation, like tracking a moving target with your eyes. But the research tells a more reassuring story. It’s a well-studied therapy for trauma, and it’s increasingly explored for anxiety and depression, too.

    Here’s what EMDR involves, what the research reveals, and what a session is like, so you have a clearer picture of whether it might make sense for you.

    It has been revealed that EMDR stands for eye movement desensitization and reprocessing. It’s a structured therapy that helps the brain reprocess distressing memories so they carry less emotional weight. Psychologist Francine Shapiro, PhD, developed it in the late 1980s after she noticed that certain eye movements seemed to ease her own troubling thoughts.

    EMDR rests on Shapiro’s adaptive information processing model. The idea is that your brain normally files an experience away, so you can recall it later without feeling like you’re living it again. But a frightening or painful event can interrupt that process, leaving the memory raw and unfiled, still carrying the fear and detail of that moment. That’s why it can resurface later, as vivid as the day it happened.

    According to this model, “processing” a memory means helping your brain finish the filing. You don’t forget what happened, and the facts don’t change. What changes is the emotional charge it carries, so recalling it feels less like reliving it and more like remembering it. To help that happen, EMDR uses a technique called “bilateral stimulation.”.

    Sources indicate that EMDR uses a technique called bilateral stimulation. While you hold a difficult memory in mind, a trained therapist guides you through side-to-side stimulation.

    Bilateral stimulation can take a few forms:.

    eye movements that follow your therapist’s fingers.

    gentle taps that switch between your hands or knees.

    tones that play in one ear, then the other.

    There’s a theory behind the side-to-side part, though researchers are still working out exactly why it helps. The leading explanation is about mental bandwidth. Your working memory, the part of your mind that holds what you’re focused on right now, can only handle so much at once. When you track side-to-side movement while recalling a hard memory, the two tasks compete for that limited space. The hard memory tends to feel a little less vivid, and with repetition it can lose its sharp edges, so it feels less overwhelming to hold.

    💙 Learn more in our guide to bilateral stimulation.

    According to recent reports, EMDR has eight phases, though they tend to blend together in practice. The early phases cover your history and teach you coping skills, so you feel prepared before any hard memories arise. In the middle phases, you focus on a specific memory while following bilateral stimulation, which is meant to help your brain reprocess it. The final phases check that the memory feels less distressing and help you close out the work safely.

    Sources indicate that the evidence is strong for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), a condition that can develop after a frightening or life-threatening event. A Cochrane review (a gold-standard summary of research on a topic) found that EMDR and trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) both reduce PTSD symptoms. They also outperformed other therapies when researchers checked in after treatment ended. A 2024 review in the Journal of Traumatic Stress identified more than 30 randomized controlled trials supporting EMDR for PTSD in adults and children. Major health organizations, including the World Health Organization, recommend EMDR for PTSD.

    It has been revealed that however, some guidelines, including those from the American Psychological Association (APA), rate the evidence for EMDR as less certain than for trauma-focused CBT. Researchers also debate exactly why EMDR works.

    💙 Read more about how EMDR can help you cope with PTSD.

    It has been revealed that the picture is more mixed outside PTSD. Early research suggests EMDR may help with anxiety, as one meta-analysis found reduced symptoms of anxiety, panic, and phobia, though the studies were small and varied in quality.

    Recent findings suggest that evidence for depression is emerging as well. Another meta-analysis showed reduced depression symptoms, with the strongest effects in more severe cases. These findings are promising, but they don’t carry the same weight as the PTSD research.

    In a recent development, after you and a therapist finish the early phases, you bring a specific memory to mind and notice the thoughts and body sensations that come with it. Then your therapist guides you through the bilateral stimulation while you let your mind go where it goes. You can ask to pause or stop at any time. Unlike many talk therapies, EMDR doesn’t require you to describe the memory in detail.

    Sessions usually run 60–90 minutes. Your therapist pauses often to check in on what you noticed. Over several rounds of bilateral stimulation, many people find the memory feels less sharp, even though the facts don’t change. Between sessions, a mindfulness practice, such as slow breathing or a body scan, can help you ease feelings that surface.

    Recent findings suggest that 💙 Explore Calm's EMDR-Inspired Bilateral: Anxiety, a set of music tracks that alternate gently between your left and right ear. It draws on the bilateral stimulation used in EMDR, though audio-only versions haven’t been studied on their own the way clinical EMDR has. Think of it as a calming complement to therapy, not a replacement for a trained therapist.

    Industry observers note that the answer varies, since it depends on what you’re working through. For a single, recent trauma, some people notice their symptoms ease within a handful of sessions. More complex or long-standing trauma usually takes longer, sometimes many months. Therapists describe a typical course as 6–12 sessions, though it varies widely from person to person.

    It has been revealed that along the way, some people feel worse before they feel better. Painful memories can stir up strong emotions in the short term, which is common and doesn’t mean EMDR isn’t working. Before reprocessing begins, your therapist teaches you coping skills, such as grounding exercises that anchor you in the present, so you have tools to use if those feelings get intense.

    💙 Try the 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 practice, a quick way to ground yourself in the present, with Prof. Megan Reitz.

    EMDR stands for eye movement desensitization and reprocessing. It’s a form of therapy that uses bilateral stimulation, such as guided eye movements, to help your brain process distressing memories so they feel less intense. Psychologist Francine Shapiro developed this therapy in the late 1980s.

    According to recent reports, EMDR may help with anxiety, though PTSD is where the evidence is strongest. The studies on anxiety are smaller and less consistent. If your anxiety is tied to a specific frightening experience, it may be worth asking a therapist whether EMDR fits your situation.

    💙 Explore how mindfulness can help you manage your anxiety.

    Industry observers note that EMDR differs from talk therapy because it doesn’t require you to describe your experience in detail. You’ll still talk with your therapist, especially early on, but the reprocessing happens while you hold a memory in mind and follow bilateral stimulation. Talk therapies like cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) focus more on examining and reshaping your thoughts out loud.

    The main benefit of EMDR is that it can ease the distress tied to painful memories. For many people with PTSD, that can mean fewer flashbacks and less of that constant, on-alert feeling.

    Much of the debate is about why EMDR works, not whether it does. The evidence is strongest for PTSD, with early and more mixed findings for anxiety and depression.

    Some studies suggest the eye movements themselves add little. The benefit may instead come from giving your mind a second task while you recall a memory, which can make it feel less vivid and emotionally intense. Other tasks that split your attention may have the same effect.

    Certain guidelines, including the APA’s, consider the evidence for EMDR less established than for trauma-focused CBT. None of this takes away from the relief many people find with EMDR. It’s useful context as you weigh your options with a therapist.

    EMDR is generally safe when a trained therapist delivers it, though you may experience some short-term effects. You might feel more emotional or tired between sessions, or have vivid dreams as your brain keeps processing the memory.

    These reactions usually pass within a day or two. If they last longer or feel overwhelming, it’s a good idea to tell your therapist, who can adjust the pace with you. Serious side effects are uncommon when a therapist follows the full eight-phase process.

    The number of sessions you need depends on the memory you’re addressing and how long it has affected you. Some people feel relief after a few sessions, while longer-standing experiences often take more time. A common range is 6–12 sessions, but your timeline may be shorter or longer. Your therapist can give you a better sense of what to expect once they know your history.

    According to recent reports, full EMDR needs a trained therapist, so it’s not something to try on your own. A therapist helps you reprocess memories and stay grounded if one feels overwhelming, which matters most with intense trauma.

    # I built a spreadsheet that attacks itself: Suture, made with Kiro.

    This post was written as part of the Kiroween 2026 hackathon.

    In a recent development, my runway model noted 21.76 months. Then I let it fuzz itself, and in about three seconds it found inputs that made runway -179.88 months, with a status cell cheerfully telling the company to "RAISE NOW". The formula was one line, =Inputs!B2/B4, and nothing about it looked wrong.

    Industry observers note that that's the kind of bug Suture finds. Here's what I built, and how Kiro shaped the way I built it.

    Sources indicate that field audits compiled by researcher Raymond Panko found errors in most of the real business spreadsheets examined. Famous failures, like the debt-and-growth paper whose average left out five countries, or the "London Whale" risk model that divided by a sum instead of an average, share one pattern: the numbers looked plausible, so nobody checked.

    Modern models make it harder still, because they mix SQL queries, Python and formulas, and no tool checks the whole chain at once.

    Suture stitches three engines into one dependency graph that runs entirely in the browser:.

    Sources indicate that in the runway model, a SQL cohort table feeds a NumPy least-squares burn projection, which feeds the runway formula. There's no server and no upload.

    Sources indicate that the Exorcist is a fuzzer built on fast-check. You declare rules ("runway >= 0") and input ranges. It pushes scenarios through all three engines, checks your rules plus five universal invariants (no NaN leaks, SQL and NumPy agreeing, results not depending on edit order…), and when something breaks it shrinks the failure to the smallest inputs that still break it.

    According to recent reports, it scales, too: a built-in audit generates 100,000 orders in DuckDB, pivots them in NumPy, and finds a real policy bug. The discount cap was applied to each discount instead of the stacked total.

    I built the whole thing in Kiro Web. Four things made the difference.

    It has been revealed that 1. Spec first. Before any code, Kiro and I wrote 5 specs with 291 acceptance criteria in EARS form ("WHEN … THE SYSTEM SHALL …"). The most notable one pinned the value contract that three engines must agree on: error codes, -0, NaN and Infinity, and who owns Arrow buffers. Every task lists the test that proves it and the commit that delivered it. One performance test stayed failing for a whole phase, with its 50 ms limit unchanged, until the spec described the incremental scheduler that fixed it. With vibe coding I would have just loosened the limit.

    According to recent reports, 2. Steering turned into checks. Three steering files hold the non-negotiables, and each rule became something a machine checks. The core package can't use DOM or Node APIs (it's a compile error), every dependency license is audited, and colors and trademarks are scanned in tests.

    3. Hooks that test while I build. A hook reruns the property tests every time the agent edits core code, and logs any fresh counterexample. Property tests caught bugs I'd never have written a unit test for: MOD(1, -3) returned the wrong sign, and a formula like AA(#N/A/FALSE) stopped parsing after it was printed.

    According to recent reports, 4. "Discuss first". I saved a rule as a Kiro learning: before any edit, propose options and trade-offs, then wait for my approval. Every phase started with a plan I agreed to, not with surprise code.

    The same engine ships as an MCP server on npm:.

    It gives Kiro four tools. The interesting one is suture_verify_patch: Kiro proposes a fix like =IF(B4<=0,120,Inputs!B2/B4), and Suture replays the counterexample against it, runs a fresh 1,000-run audit, and reports counterexampleFixed: true with zero regressions. The agent proves the fix instead of guessing.

    I also built Suture Crew, a Kiro Crew app with three agents. Schema Archaeologist maps lineage, Invariant Adversary runs the fuzzer and posts X-Ray links, and Formula Surgeon only recommends a fix after it's been proven. It has a nightly schedule and a dashboard.

    I'm a student at Mizoram University, and this is the biggest project I've built. I'd love feedback!

    #139069. About 5,000 of 100,000 Zero-Edge Strategies Pass p < 0.05: A Multiple-Testing Check in Python

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (408 w)

    About 5,000 of 100,000 Zero-Edge Strategies Pass p < 0.05: A Multiple-Testing Check in Python

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (408 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that suppose you backtest 100,000 strategies that have zero edge.
    • In a recent development, A post on X describes an open strategy library, "every single one fully backtested on years of real market data." I haven't checked that claim.
    • According to recent reports, each row is one strategy with zero-mean daily returns.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that suppose you backtest 100,000 strategies that have zero edge. On average about 5,000 of them pass a one-sided p < 0.05 test by luck alone. At p < 0.01 about 1,000 still pass, and at p < 0.001 about 100. A Bonferroni cut for the whole scan, 0.05/100,000 = 5e-7, brings the expected number of lucky passes down to 0.05. (100,000 is my own example scale.).

    In a recent development, A post on X describes an open strategy library, "every single one fully backtested on years of real market data." I haven't checked that claim. A long list of backtested winners tells you nothing about edge until you know N.

    According to recent reports, each row is one strategy with zero-mean daily returns. A one-sided t-test checks whether the mean is above zero.

    In a recent development, the expected column is N × alpha, so the number of lucky winners grows linearly with N. Under independence, the count at 0.05 has a standard deviation of about 69.

    Industry observers note that N covers every rule, parameter set, market and timeframe you tried, including the ones you dropped. If N × threshold comes out in the thousands, a leaderboard with thousands of winners is exactly what noise alone would give you.

    Recent findings suggest that A holdout period that played no part in selection removes most of the lucky winners, but with thousands of survivors it still lets hundreds through at an uncorrected threshold. Re-test the 5,000 zero-edge survivors at an uncorrected p < 0.05 and about 250 pass again. Divide by the survivor count instead, 0.05/5,000 = 1e-5, and the expected number of false survivors drops to about 0.05.

    These are expected values for simulated noise (zero edge, normally distributed returns, no trading costs), and I didn't run the code, so the passed counts will differ from the expected column and change with the seed. Real strategies are often highly correlated, which puts the effective number of independent tests below N: the expected count is still N × alpha, but a single scan's count swings more, and 0.05/N ends up stricter than it needs to be.

    For your own scan: count N, multiply it by your threshold before you look at the leaderboard, and re-test every survivor on an unused holdout at 0.05 divided by the number of survivors you carry into it.

    Best Way to Evaluate Mobile Hardware Tradeoffs in 2026

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2963 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Canonical version: https://thelooplet.com/posts/best-way-to-evaluate-mobile-hardware-tradeoffs-in-2026.
    • TL;DR: Mobile hardware in 2026 is splitting into two opposing directions—Apple adding precision and volume to AirTag 2 while Samsung strips telephoto range and laser autofocus from the S27 Ultra—so architects must evaluate device refresh cycles by feature regression risk, not just generation number.
    • Mobile hardware evaluation in 2026 can no longer rely on the assumption that newer flagship devices are strictly superior to their predecessors.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Canonical version: https://thelooplet.com/posts/best-way-to-evaluate-mobile-hardware-tradeoffs-in-2026.

    TL;DR: Mobile hardware in 2026 is splitting into two opposing directions—Apple adding precision and volume to AirTag 2 while Samsung strips telephoto range and laser autofocus from the S27 Ultra—so architects must evaluate device refresh cycles by feature regression risk, not just generation number.

    Mobile hardware evaluation in 2026 can no longer rely on the assumption that newer flagship devices are strictly superior to their predecessors. The market has bifurcated. On one side, Apple is shipping the AirTag 2 with a second-generation Ultra Wideband chip and a significantly louder speaker, expanding the usable envelope for Precision Finding and audio-based discovery. On the other side, Samsung is reportedly removing the laser autofocus sensor and the 3x telephoto lens from the Galaxy S27 Ultra, collapsing optical capabilities that existed on the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Meanwhile, Android security patch volumes remain high—179 fixes in a single November 2026 bulletin for the Galaxy S23 series—demonstrating that software support longevity and hardware capability are decoupled metrics.

    Industry observers note that this article provides a framework for evaluating these tradeoffs. It covers Ultra Wideband ranging physics, speaker acoustics in accessory design, camera sensor tradeoffs, computational autofocus limitations, security patch cadence, and device refresh-cycle planning. Each section includes concrete implementation details, code-adjacent examples, tradeoff analysis, and practical guidance for engineering teams building mobile applications, accessory integrations, or device fleets.

    Apple shipped AirTag 2 in November 2026 after a five-year gap between generations, pricing the 1-pack at $18 and the 4-pack at a reduced rate from the prior $29 baseline, according to 9to5Mac. The headline change is a second-generation Ultra Wideband (UWB) chip that extends Precision Finding to roughly 1.5 times the distance of the original AirTag. That is not a marginal silicon refresh. Precision Finding on the first-generation AirTag required users to be in fairly close proximity before step-by-step directional guidance became available. By pushing the usable envelope outward, Apple makes the feature trigger in far more real-world scenarios, which changes how developers should think about accessory proximity assumptions in Find My integrations.

    Ultra Wideband operates by measuring time-of-flight between radio pulses across a wide spectrum of frequencies. The original AirTag used a first-generation UWB implementation that provided sub-meter precision but only within a limited radius—typically on the order of a few meters indoors before multipath interference and signal attenuation degraded the confidence of directional arrows. The second-generation chip in AirTag 2 improves both the signal-to-noise ratio and the ranging algorithm, effectively extending the distance at which the iPhone can resolve direction and distance with sufficient confidence to display Precision Finding UI.

    From an integration standpoint, this means your application’s discovery logic should not assume a fixed discovery radius. If your Find My accessory integration at the moment triggers “nearby” states at, say, 5 meters, AirTag 2 may begin reporting directional guidance at 7.5 meters or more depending on environmental conditions. That 1.5x multiplier is an approximate baseline; actual range varies with obstructions, device orientation, and interference from other 2.4 GHz radios.

    Teams integrating with the Find My accessory framework should treat AirTag 2 as a different hardware class than the original. The following considerations apply to your discovery state machine:.

    Discovery radius: Review any hardcoded constants that define “nearby” or “in-range” thresholds. If your UI highlights a “Get Directions” button only when the accessory is within 4 meters, that threshold may now fire too late for AirTag 2 users who could have begun precision finding at 6 meters.

    Sources indicate that directional UI timing: Precision Finding relies on the iPhone’s UWB antenna array to compute angle of arrival. With extended range, the directional arrow may appear while the user is still moving through a large space. Your onboarding or tutorial screens should set expectations that guidance can begin farther from the accessory than it did with the original AirTag.

    In a recent development, background vs. foreground behavior: Extended range increases the likelihood that an accessory is detected while the app is in the background. Ensure your background location and accessory monitoring entitlements are configured to handle the increased frequency of proximity events without draining battery.

    Sources indicate that the second major change is a built-in speaker that Apple claims is 50 percent louder than the original, enabling audible detection from up to twice as far away. For anyone building applications that rely on audio cues for lost-item recovery, this alters the acoustic design space. A louder speaker increases the probability of detection through fabric, bags, or couch cushions, but it also raises the noise floor for consumers in quiet environments.

    Teams integrating with the Find My accessory framework should treat the AirTag 2 speaker as a different hardware class than the original, with adjusted expectations for sound-trigger latency and effective range. Specifically:.

    Sound-trigger latency: A louder speaker may require different drive circuitry or amplifier behavior. If your application measures the time between issuing a play-sound command and receiving an auditory confirmation (via user feedback or secondary device detection), recalibrate those latency expectations.

    Effective range through obstructions: Doubling audible range does not mean linear penetration through all materials. Dense materials such as leather, thick denim, or water-containing objects still attenuate high-frequency sound. Test audio detection in realistic scenarios—inside a backpack, under a couch cushion, in a coat pocket—rather than relying on open-air specifications.

    Recent findings suggest that user experience in quiet environments: A 50 percent louder speaker can be disruptive in libraries, offices, or bedrooms. If your application allows users to trigger sound remotely, consider adding volume profiles or “quiet mode” toggles that respect environmental context.

    From an engineering standpoint, these two improvements stack. Extended Precision Finding range narrows the search area before the user even begins listening, while the louder speaker shortens the final localization phase once the user is nearby. That compounding effect means AirTag 2 is not simply a faster version of the same product; it is a different class of tracker with different integration assumptions. Any architecture that caches last-known location or assumes a fixed discovery radius needs to be revisited when the underlying hardware can report from significantly farther away.

    Recent findings suggest that samsung is taking the opposite approach with the Galaxy S27 Ultra, expected to launch early next year. According to reporting by Gizmodo citing leaker Ice Universe, the S27 Ultra will drop the laser autofocus sensor that has accompanied Samsung rear camera systems since the Galaxy S21 Ultra in 2021. The sensor projects infrared light onto subjects to improve focus speed and accuracy, particularly in low-light conditions. Without it, Samsung will reportedly rely on AI focus technology, shifting autofocus from a dedicated hardware measurement to a computational inference problem.

    Industry observers note that laser autofocus emits an infrared pulse toward the subject and measures the reflection time to determine distance. This distance measurement is fed to the lens actuator to drive focus directly, rather than relying on contrast detection or phase detection from the image sensor alone. The benefits are most pronounced in:.

    According to recent reports, low-light scenes: Contrast-based autofocus struggles when there is little luminance detail. Laser AF provides an independent distance cue.

    Moving subjects: Direct distance measurement can reduce focus hunting compared to iterative contrast adjustments.

    Close-range macro: At very short distances, depth-of-field is shallow and focus accuracy is critical; laser ranging reduces the feedback loop.

    Sources indicate that removing this sensor means the S27 Ultra must rely on dual-pixel phase detection, contrast detection, and computational inference from the image sensor itself. In well-lit conditions, modern sensor-phase autofocus is often sufficient. In low light, however, the absence of an active ranging system introduces focus latency and inconsistency.

    Recent findings suggest that the same report indicates the S27 Ultra will lose its 10-megapixel 3x telephoto lens, leaving only a single 5x telephoto option. The current Galaxy S26 Ultra ships with both a 3x and a 5x telephoto, giving photographers two distinct optical reach points. Removing the 3x collapses that range into a single telephoto focal length, which forces digital cropping or computational interpolation for intermediate distances.

    Industry observers note that for mobile developers building camera-intensive applications, this is a hardware regression disguised as a generational upgrade. Consider the following impact on common workflows:.

    Document scanning: A 3x optical module is often ideal for capturing letter-sized documents at a comfortable working distance without distortion. A 5x module forces the user farther back, increasing the chance of perspective skew and requiring more physical space. Digital cropping from the main sensor to simulate 3x loses resolution and increases noise.

    Barcode and QR code capture: At intermediate distances (1–2 meters), a 3x optical telephoto provides a magnified, high-resolution view of the code. Relying on the main sensor with digital zoom reduces the effective pixel density on the target, potentially increasing scan failure rates.

    In a recent development, augmented reality: AR applications that place virtual objects at specific real-world distances benefit from discrete optical focal lengths. A single 5x telephoto creates a gap in the 2x–4x range where the application must choose between wide-angle distortion or upscaled digital crop.

    Samsung’s reported shift to “AI focus technology” replaces a hardware measurement with software inference. This tradeoff deserves scrutiny:.

    | Factor | Laser Autofocus (Hardware) | AI/Computational Focus (Software) |.

    |--------|---------------------------|-----------------------------------|.

    | Measurement basis | Direct infrared time-of-flight | Image sensor data + neural network inference |.

    | Low-light performance | Strong; independent of scene illumination | Weaker; depends on sensor noise and available light |.

    | Latency | Deterministic, fast | Variable; depends on inference pipeline |.

    | Determinism | Consistent across similar distances | Can vary with scene content, motion, and lighting |.

    | Hardware cost | Additional sensor, calibration, board space | Software development and compute cycles |.

    For applications where focus speed and repeatability matter—such as industrial inspection, document digitization, or AR object tracking—the S27 Ultra’s reliance on computational focus introduces non-deterministic behavior that is difficult to compensate for in software.

    Gizmodo also notes that the S27 Ultra design reportedly moves to an edge-to-edge camera plateau similar to recent iPhone Pro models, but unlike Apple’s implementation, which houses the chipset and aids thermal management, Samsung’s version is described as largely cosmetic, with much of the right side of the module empty. That design choice signals a prioritization of visual consistency over engineering density, which matters for device thermals and internal space allocation in any application that sustains heavy camera or sensor usage.

    If your application records 4K video, runs continuous computer vision, or performs real-time AR tracking, thermal throttling becomes a concern. A cosmetic camera plateau that does not contribute to heat dissipation means the SoC and camera subsystems must rely on other thermal pathways. In sustained workloads, this can lead to frame drops, reduced camera frame rates, or throttled image processing pipelines.

    According to recent reports, the Galaxy S23 series received the November 2026 Android security enhancement with 179 fixes, according to Android Headlines. That volume of patches in a single monthly cycle underscores the attack surface present in modern mobile SoCs, modem firmware, and the broader Android ecosystem. For teams managing fleets of Android devices, a 179-fix security bulletin is not routine maintenance; it is a signal that significant portions of the platform require continuous remediation.

    A monthly security bulletin of this magnitude typically includes patches for:.

    Kernel vulnerabilities: Privilege escalation, memory corruption, and driver flaws in the Linux kernel.

    Media framework components: Codecs and parsers that process untrusted video, audio, and image data.

    Modem and baseband firmware: Remote code execution risks in cellular connectivity stacks.

    Qualcomm, Samsung, or MediaTek proprietary components: Vendor-specific drivers and trustlets.

    Android framework services: System server, package manager, and permission model flaws.

    For enterprise mobility management (EMM) teams, this patch volume has direct operational consequences:.

    Testing burden: Each monthly patch requires regression testing of enterprise apps, VPN profiles, and security policies before deployment.

    Industry observers note that revision latency: Carriers and OEMs often delay security patches by weeks or months. A 179-fix bulletin released in November may not reach end-user devices until December or January.

    In a recent development, compliance reporting: Regulated industries (healthcare, finance, government) may need to document patch levels for audited devices. High patch volume increases the complexity of compliance reporting.

    This patch cadence creates tension with the S27 Ultra feature removals. Samsung is removing hardware capabilities from its flagship while still shipping devices that require nearly two hundred security fixes per month on supported older models. Architects evaluating Samsung hardware for enterprise or consumer deployments must weigh reduced camera capability against an unchanged, high-volume security maintenance burden. The patch volume also implies that device longevity is tied more to software support policy than to camera hardware completeness, which should factor into refresh-cycle planning.

    Industry observers note that the mobile hardware market is diverging by philosophy, and teams that assume generational parity will make incorrect procurement and integration decisions. Apple is adding measurable performance to a low-cost accessory, while Samsung is subtracting optical capabilities from its premium phone. My opinion is that the S27 Ultra represents a shrinkflation trap for camera-dependent applications: removing the 3x telephoto and laser autofocus forces developers to compensate with software workarounds that will never match dedicated optics, and relying on AI focus for low-light scenarios introduces latency and inconsistency that hardware autofocus avoided. I predict teams building AR, document scanning, or barcode capture workflows on Android will explicitly avoid the S27 Ultra or pin minimum device requirements to the S26 Ultra and earlier.

    For iOS accessory developers, AirTag 2 changes the proximity model. I believe the 1.5x Precision Finding range extension and doubled speaker audibility make AirTag 2 the default recommendation for any Find My accessory integration, and supporting the original AirTag as a fallback should be treated as legacy device maintenance rather than a first-class target. Teams should audit their assumed discovery radii and audio-trigger logic against AirTag 2 specifications before the next app release cycle.

    When evaluating mobile hardware for your application or fleet in 2026, use the following framework to avoid generation-number bias.

    According to recent reports, never assume that a newer flagship contains all sensors from its predecessor. Before certifying a device for camera-intensive workloads, verify:.

    Telephoto focal lengths and megapixel counts.

    Presence of dedicated autofocus hardware (laser, phase detection pixels, or both).

    LiDAR or depth sensor availability for AR applications.

    UWB chip generation for accessory ranging.

    | Requirement | Galaxy S26 Ultra | Galaxy S27 Ultra (reported) | Decision |.

    |-------------|------------------|----------------------------|----------|.

    | 3x optical telephoto | Yes | No | S26 Ultra preferred |.

    | 5x optical telephoto | Yes | Yes | Parity |.

    | Laser autofocus | Yes | No | S26 Ultra preferred for low light |.

    | Main sensor resolution | 200 MP | TBD | Verify at launch |.

    For Find My and UWB accessory integrations, define discovery zones as configurable ranges:.

    Immediate zone: 0–1.5 meters (haptic feedback, sound trigger).

    Near zone: 1.5–5 meters (directional arrow, proximity UI).

    Extended zone: 5–7.5+ meters (AirTag 2 Precision Finding may activate).

    Store these values in remote configuration rather than hardcoded constants so you can adjust per hardware generation without an app store enhancement.

    If your application triggers accessory sounds, build in fallback logic:.

    Detect accessory generation if the framework exposes it.

    Adjust volume expectations: AirTag 2 is louder; original AirTag may not penetrate thick fabric.

    Provide user guidance: “Move closer if you do not hear the sound” rather than assuming hardware failure.

    For Android fleets, evaluate devices based on:.

    Length of promised security update support.

    Historical speed of patch delivery from OEM and carrier.

    Ease of mobile device management (MDM) enrollment and policy enforcement.

    End-of-life date for the specific model.

    A device with a weaker camera but three more years of guaranteed patches may be the better enterprise choice than a flagship with superior optics but uncertain support.

    If you must support devices lacking dedicated hardware (e.g., S27 Ultra without laser AF or 3x telephoto), test the following in realistic conditions:.

    Low-light focus speed and success rate.

    Digital zoom image quality at 2x–3x equivalent.

    Barcode scan reliability at intermediate distances.

    AR plane detection stability without LiDAR.

    Document failure modes and decide whether software compensation is acceptable or whether the device should be excluded from your supported matrix.

    Industry observers note that different workloads prioritize different hardware capabilities. The table below summarizes how the 2026 hardware shifts affect common mobile application domains.

    | Domain | AirTag 2 Impact | S27 Ultra Impact | Recommendation |.

    |--------|----------------|------------------|----------------|.

    | Lost-item recovery | Positive: longer UWB range, louder speaker | N/A | Target AirTag 2; treat original as legacy |.

    | Document scanning | N/A | Negative: no 3x telephoto, no laser AF | Pin to S26 Ultra or test digital zoom heavily |.

    | Barcode capture | N/A | Negative: reduced optical reach at intermediate distances | Test scan rates; avoid S27 Ultra for warehouse use |.

    | AR / spatial computing | N/A | Negative: no laser AF, potential thermal limits | Verify depth sensing and focus behavior |.

    | General consumer apps | Neutral | Neutral | Standard generational evaluation applies |.

    | Enterprise fleet | N/A | Mixed: security support matters more than camera | Prioritize patch longevity over optics |.

    AWS Security Alerts in an Afternoon: 5 Audit Commands and One CloudFormation Template

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (876 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that on November 28, 2025, Sysdig watched an attacker take test credentials from a public S3 bucket and have their own code running in the victim's Lambda function eight minutes later.
    • Industry observers note that that is fast, but it is not unusual.
    • This post is the setup I would do in an afternoon instead:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that on November 28, 2025, Sysdig watched an attacker take test credentials from a public S3 bucket and have their own code running in the victim's Lambda function eight minutes later. Admin access followed in under ten.

    Industry observers note that that is fast, but it is not unusual. Unit 42 leaked keys to public GitHub on purpose and saw them used within five minutes. Clutch Security measured 6.6 minutes on average.

    Most of us have no security team. This post is the setup I would do in an afternoon instead:.

    Recent findings suggest that prices are for US East (N. Virginia), read on November 26, 2026.

    CloudTrail delivers within about 5 minutes of an API call on average, and AWS indicates that time is not guaranteed. So this pipeline tells you at roughly minute five. Keep that number in mind for the last section.

    All five commands are read-only.

    According to recent reports, cloudTrail's free 90-day event history already holds a lot. This is one account's console sign-ins, with the names changed. Two rows are the root user, and nothing on this page tells anyone.

    Two results look like failures and are really findings:.

    Create the trail in the console. The docs say all trails created there are multi-Region, and the console sets up the bucket policy for you.

    GuardDuty has to be enabled per Region. The Regions you never deploy to are the ones an attacker will use, so enable all of them:.

    In a recent development, that loop changes your account, and the 30-day trial starts per Region when you run it. Check the Usage page in the GuardDuty console before the trial ends.

    Save this as aws-security-alerts.yaml.

    Deploy it in us-east-1 first (see trap 1 below), then confirm the subscription email SNS sends you:.

    According to recent reports, what I verified, and what I did not. The template passes aws cloudformation validate-template, and both event patterns matched the right sample events in the test below. I have not deployed this exact stack to a live account, so I have not watched an email arrive from it. Deploy it to a sandbox account first.

    In a recent development, attachUserPolicy earns its place twice. It also fires when AWS quarantines a leaked key, because the quarantine is a policy attached to the user. The policy ARN is in the event's requestParameters.

    Recent findings suggest that some of these are noisy on a busy account. AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress fires for every rule, not just 0.0.0.0/0. Start with everything, then trim what your own pipeline does every day.

    aws events test-event-pattern checks a pattern against a sample event without creating anything. This is how I tested the sign-in rule:.

    In a recent development, I ran nine cases across the two rules. Root sign-in, IAM user without MFA, StopLogging and CreateAccessKey matched. An IAM user with MFA, a failed login, a single sign-on session and DescribeInstances did not.

    It has been revealed that 1. IAM lives in us-east-1. IAM, STS and CloudFront are global services, and CloudTrail records their events in US East (N. Virginia). A rule in eu-west-1 will never see CreateAccessKey. Root sign-ins land in us-east-1, us-east-2 or us-west-2. Deploy the stack in us-east-1, then in those two, then in every Region you run workloads in.

    According to recent reports, 2. MFAUsed is always No for single sign-on. AWS only sets it for IAM users and root. Without the IAMUser filter, every SSO login emails you.

    3. S3 event names differ from the API. The API call DeletePublicAccessBlock appears in CloudTrail as DeleteBucketPublicAccessBlock or DeleteAccountPublicAccessBlock. Match the CloudTrail name.

    4. Read-only calls need a different rule state. A rule in the default ENABLED state does not match read-only management events. To alert on something like GetSecretValue, set the rule's state to ENABLED_WITH_ALL_CLOUDTRAIL_MANAGEMENT_EVENTS. You also need a trail that is logging, or none of these rules receive anything.

    One more: the docs spell the sign-in detail-type two ways (AWS Console Sign In via CloudTrail and AWS Console Signin via CloudTrail). The pattern above matches on source: aws.signin so it does not depend on either.

    AWS shipped two things that cover some of this:.

    You now get an email at about minute five. It is a block of JSON. It does not say whether that CreateAccessKey was your deploy pipeline or a stranger, and at 3 a.m. nobody reads it until morning.

    That gap is the real work. Someone has to look at who did it, from where, and what else they did in the same few minutes. Staffing that around the clock takes 4.2 people per seat (168 hours in a week, 40 in a working one), which is about $542,556 a year at the US median analyst wage.

    Recent findings suggest that disclosure: I work on Jutsu, which does that first investigation in software and asks before it acts. The longer version of this post, with the cost comparison and screenshots, is on the Jutsu blog.

    Sources indicate that whatever you choose, decide who answers the alert. A rule nobody reads is a log.

    What would you add to the event list? I left out RunInstances and PutRolePolicy to keep the noise down, and I am not sure that was right.

    According to recent reports, that’s why I built Browsedown. Right-click your docs/ folder in VS Code and choose Open in Browser. It serves the Markdown locally and opens your README in a browser tab, with the subfolders in a sidebar. There’s nothing to configure or push first.

    #139062. Giving a coding agent test results it can act on: JUnit XML, go test -json and a short failure summary

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (673 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

    Giving a coding agent test results it can act on: JUnit XML, go test -json and a short failure summary

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (673 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Most coding agents spend a large share of their turns in one loop: change code, run the tests, read the result, change code again.
    • Recent findings suggest that test runners already know the answer in structured form.
    • Three common runners, each writing a report next to its normal output:.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Most coding agents spend a large share of their turns in one loop: change code, run the tests, read the result, change code again. The quality of that loop depends on what "read the result" means. An exit code of 1 tells the model something failed and nothing about what. The full log tells it everything, at a cost in tokens and attention, and the one assertion that matters is somewhere in the middle.

    Recent findings suggest that test runners already know the answer in structured form. Most can write a report that lists every test, its status, and for each failure a message and a stack trace. This post indicates how to get those reports out of a sandbox and turn them into a tool result built for a model: the counts, the first few failures, and a clear signal when the run did not finish at all.

    Three common runners, each writing a report next to its normal output:.

    Recent findings suggest that jest can write the same JUnit XML through the separately installed jest-junit reporter. JUnit XML is the closest thing the ecosystem has to a shared format: a testsuite holds testcase elements, and a failing case has a failure or error child with a message attribute and the trace as text. Skipped cases have a skipped child.

    Go's format is a stream instead. Each line is an event with an Action such as run, output, pass, fail or skip, plus the Package and Test it belongs to. A test's output arrives as a series of output events before its fail.

    The parser below reads either format and returns the same shape: totals, the first five failures, and how many more were left out. Each failure's message and details are cut to a fixed size. It uses the fast-xml-parser package for XML.

    A few choices here are deliberate:.

    The tool that runs the tests should distinguish three outcomes, because the right next step is different for each:.

    It has been revealed that here is that tool for pytest with the Sandscale TypeScript SDK. run returns exitCode, stdout, stderr, timedOut and oomKilled, and readFile reads the report back:.

    In a recent development, the stale report is deleted before each run. Without that, a run that crashes before pytest writes anything would read the previous run's report and tell the model its tests failed for old reasons, or passed.

    According to recent reports, combine the exit code with the report rather than trusting either alone. A runner can exit non-zero with no failing tests listed, for example pytest exits with a distinct code when it collected no tests at all, and the summary's total of zero is the clue the model needs.

    Industry observers note that once the model knows which test failed, it rarely needs the whole suite again. Say so in the tool description, and give it a way to rerun a subset:.

    Narrow reruns are cheaper and give shorter, clearer reports. Run the full suite again before the agent declares the task done.

    Everything in this post runs inside the sandbox, under the agent's control. That is the right place for the edit-test loop, and the wrong place to decide whether a change is safe to merge. An agent can edit a test until it passes, mark it skipped, or change the configuration that decides which tests run. None of that is malicious; it is what optimizing for "tests pass" looks like.

    In a recent development, A Sandscale sandbox gives each run its own Firecracker microVM, so test suites the agent wrote or changed run against their own kernel and filesystem, with the network mode defaulting to none. The builtin:base template has Python 3, Node.js, Git and a C compiler; your project's own test dependencies go in with the project. The result fields this post relies on, exitCode, timedOut and oomKilled, come straight from run, and the command and the files read back are recorded in the audit log.

    Originally published on the Sandscale blog.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you want to remove vocals from a song, isolate drums, or export several instrument tracks, sending audio to a third-party API is not your only option.
    • This tutorial uses the project's stable v1.0.0 release and Docker Compose.
    • Recent findings suggest that clone the repository, start the default Compose service, open http://localhost:7860, and upload an MP3, WAV, FLAC, M4A, AAC, OGG, or OPUS file.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you want to remove vocals from a song, isolate drums, or export several instrument tracks, sending audio to a third-party API is not your only option. Stem Separator is an open-source, self-hosted web application that runs the separation pipeline on your own machine, homelab, or NAS.

    This tutorial uses the project's stable v1.0.0 release and Docker Compose. You will start the CPU version, verify its health endpoint, upload a supported audio file through the browser, and understand when the NVIDIA GPU configuration is appropriate.

    Recent findings suggest that clone the repository, start the default Compose service, open http://localhost:7860, and upload an MP3, WAV, FLAC, M4A, AAC, OGG, or OPUS file. The default mode separates vocals and music. Stem Separator stores model weights in a named Docker volume and writes job output to ./data/output.

    Recent findings suggest that the key boundary is that this is local processing, not an anonymous public service. The application does not include built-in authentication or rate limiting, so keep it on localhost or a trusted LAN unless you add an authenticated reverse proxy.

    The CPU deployment includes FFmpeg in the image. You do not need to install Python, PyTorch, or FFmpeg on the host for this path.

    Industry observers note that the repository is MIT licensed and the stable release used here is v1.0.0. The project README is the source for the commands and configuration discussed below: paladini/stem-separator.

    Clone the repository and build the service:.

    The service listens on port 7860. Open http://localhost:7860 in a browser.

    Sources indicate that the first build can take time because the image installs dependencies. The first separation can also take longer while the selected model downloads.

    Check the container and its health endpoint:.

    Recent findings suggest that A healthy response reports the detected device, whether FFmpeg is available, and the active and queued job counts. If FFmpeg is unavailable, the endpoint reports a degraded state instead of pretending that a separation can succeed.

    Inspect the application logs while the first model is loading:.

    Recent findings suggest that stop following the logs with Ctrl+C. The container keeps running.

    Recent findings suggest that in the web interface, select an audio file and choose a separation goal. The default Vocals & Music mode uses the curated MDX-Net Inst HQ 3 model and produces vocals and music tracks. The interface only exposes tracks that the selected model can produce, which avoids requesting outputs that the model cannot generate.

    Choose an output format supported by the application:.

    Submit the job and wait for the stages shown in the interface: preparing audio, loading the model, separating tracks, and exporting files. When processing finishes, preview tracks in the browser or download individual files and the ZIP archive.

    According to recent reports, the default Compose file maps the host directory ./data/output to /data/output in the container. That directory holds job state and exported tracks, so the results remain available when the container restarts. Model weights use the named volume stem-separator-models, which prevents a model from being downloaded again after every container recreation.

    The default Compose configuration is intentionally conservative:.

    These settings cap upload size and duration, reject jobs when disk space is too low, limit concurrent processing to one job, and bound the waiting queue. Completed or failed job folders are retained for 24 hours by default.

    Sources indicate that the default model is a practical CPU starting point. The repository also documents a BS-Roformer model of about 610 MB, recommended for an NVIDIA GPU because CPU processing can be slow. Model file size is not the same as runtime memory, so treat the RAM and VRAM guidance as a baseline, not a guarantee.

    The project provides a separate Compose override for NVIDIA CUDA. The host needs an updated NVIDIA driver and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit installation. Verify that Docker can see the GPU before starting Stem Separator:.

    Then start the GPU image with both Compose files:.

    The override replaces the CPU image, requests all GPUs, and keeps the same port and mounts. Do not run both stacks in the same checkout because both publish port 7860.

    The Docker configuration supports CPU and NVIDIA CUDA deployments. The README does not claim verified Docker acceleration for Apple Silicon MPS/CoreML, AMD ROCm, Intel graphics, or Windows DirectML. If you need those paths, evaluate the native Python setup separately instead of assuming the Docker image will pass through the host accelerator.

    It has been revealed that stem Separator places a small web application in front of python-audio-separator. Its catalog maps friendly goals such as Vocals & Music to a verified model and a set of output tracks. The job manager validates the input, creates an isolated job directory, runs the engine, and exposes status and download endpoints.

    That separation is useful operationally. A malformed filename or unsupported extension can be rejected before inference, and a low-disk condition can stop a job before it consumes more storage. Engine failures can return as actionable application errors rather than unfiltered stack traces.

    Check the logs and verify that the container has its bundled FFmpeg available. For a native Python installation, install FFmpeg and confirm that both ffmpeg and ffprobe are on PATH. A degraded health response is a signal to fix the media dependency before submitting a job.

    The first use of a model downloads its weights. Watch docker compose logs -f, check available disk space, and remember that the model cache is mounted at /data/models. Deleting the named volume forces the downloads again.

    It has been revealed that start with the default Vocals & Music model, reduce concurrency if you changed it, or choose the Force CPU option exposed by the application. The larger studio model and multi-instrument modes need more memory. A GPU does not remove the need to size the host and its VRAM correctly.

    Sources indicate that run docker compose ps and inspect the port mapping. If another application owns port 7860, change the host side of the mapping in a local Compose override, then use the matching browser URL. Keep the container port at 7860 unless you also change the health check and application configuration consistently.

    The README documents local processing, filename sanitization, isolated UUID job directories, and path-containment checks for downloads. These safeguards are not a complete deployment security model.

    There is no built-in authentication or per-IP rate limiting. Do not expose this service directly to the public internet. If remote access is necessary, put it behind a reverse proxy with HTTPS, authentication, request-size limits, and rate limits. Also review the licenses and usage rights for the audio files and model weights you process.

    In a recent development, the project is designed to process audio locally. In the Docker workflow, input files, model inference, and exports stay in the host's container volumes unless you add another integration yourself.

    It has been revealed that no. The CPU Compose file is the default. A compatible NVIDIA GPU can accelerate supported workloads, but it adds host driver and toolkit requirements.

    It has been revealed that run docker compose down. The named model volume and the ./data/output bind mount remain unless you explicitly remove them.

    According to recent reports, stem Separator turns local audio stem separation into a repeatable Docker workflow: one Compose command, a browser interface, persistent model storage, bounded jobs, and explicit CPU/GPU tradeoffs. Start with the CPU deployment, verify /health, and move to the NVIDIA override only when the host prerequisites and memory budget are clear.

    What would make a self-hosted separator more useful for your workflow: batch-folder processing, an authenticated multi-user mode, or a more detailed quality comparison between models?

    Breaking: What Couples Married For 40 Years Do When Life Gets Hard

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.
    • Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.
    • When people in decades-long marriages describe what helped them through a crisis, most of the responses they give involve leaning on each other.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

    Couples married for decades reveal what they turned to when they thought their marriage might end.

    When people in decades-long marriages describe what helped them through a crisis, most of the responses they give involve leaning on each other.

    They describe listening to each other, talking through painful subjects and sometimes having the same argument more than once.

    The researchers suggest that this response grows out of years of knowing they can count on their partner.

    In attachment theory, a partner can act as a safe haven, someone whose presence makes it easier to bear distress.

    Getting through a difficult period together may deepen that trust, making it easier to ask for help the next time it is needed.

    Dr Christian Heim, the study’s first author, and Dr Caroline Heim, study co-author, interviewed each couple together, asking each person to describe what had put their marriage under strain and what had helped them cope.

    The 180 participants were born in 24 countries and, with a few exceptions, had been married for at least 40 years.

    Around two-thirds of the couples described a threat they believed could have ended their marriage, such as the death or serious illness of a child, infidelity or prolonged periods apart.

    Talking, listening and arguing accounted for almost a quarter of the coping responses the researchers recorded.

    After an affair, some couples described arguing over it repeatedly, while bereaved partners sometimes waited for a moment when both felt able to speak.

    One partner in an American couple married for 45 years recalled asking their spouse about the son they had lost.

    It has been revealed that “Can I talk about our son? I’m hurting. Is it okay to talk about it?”.

    Some partners described taking time to grieve separately before they were ready to turn to each other.

    Around four in five coping responses involved leaning on the relationship, whether by drawing closer, persevering as a couple or giving up something one partner wanted.

    The interviews capture what couples in lasting marriages felt had helped them, leaving open whether the same approaches would have helped couples who separated.

    When partners see a problem as something they face together, they may spend less time working out who is to blame and more time trying to understand what the other person is going through.

    A previous analysis involving almost 18,000 people found that coping together and helping a partner manage stress were both linked to greater relationship satisfaction (Falconier et al., 2015).

    Some couples in the interviews felt that an illness, a bereavement or a family conflict had left them closer, even though the experience itself had been painful.

    A British couple married for 60 years described how they got through a serious conflict with their in-laws:.

    The study was published in the journal The American Journal of Family Therapy (Heim & Heim, 2025).

    Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you have ever tried running a heavy JavaScript obfuscator on a real production app, you already know the two usual outcomes:.

    Sources indicate that and on top of that, traditional variable renaming (a, _0x1f2a) barely slows down modern reverse-engineering workflows anymore. Frontier LLMs paired with AST analyzers, decompilers (Ghidra, WABT, ILSpy), and SMT solvers like Z3 reconstruct clean-room source code from minified bundles in minutes.

    According to recent reports, over the past few months at Soltrix Studios, we built Syferit, an open-core, 100% offline build-time code defense engine. We just shipped Syferit v2.1.1, and rather than just writing marketing claims about it, we put it through two real tests: a massive production Next.js app and a public 60 FPS JS + WebAssembly crackme.

    Here is what changed in v2.1, what actually broke along the way, and where you can try breaking it yourself.

    When we ran early v2.0 builds on a real production Next.js codebase (209 chunks including heavy dependencies like three.js and @ffmpeg/ffmpeg), we hit a wall:.

    That benchmark forced three real engineering fixes in Syferit v2.1.1:.

    The result on that exact same 209-chunk Next.js app:.

    Syferit runs strictly at build time (zero runtime dependencies, zero network calls, zero telemetry). Out of the box, its default v2-quantum-rns preset hardens production builds across four layers:.

    Client-side code still has to run inside V8 on the user's machine. Nothing on earth makes browser JavaScript "100% unbreakable." A determined reverse engineer with Chrome DevTools, Frida, or enough time can still set breakpoints on DOM mutations or inspect fetch() payloads at the network boundary.

    The real goal of Syferit is raising the cost of static analysis, automated AI cloning agents, and casual decompilation from "5 minutes with an LLM" to "serious manual reverse engineering," while keeping build times fast and runtime overhead near zero.

    Instead of asking anyone to take our word on runtime overhead, we built a live 60 FPS browser game and crackme called SYFER-DRIFT: The Enclave Heist:.

    Every single frame at 60 FPS, the game runs a cross-runtime JavaScript + WebAssembly verification pass protected by stock Syferit v2.1.1. There is also a "Run 1,000x Enclave Burst" button right in the telemetry bar so you can measure live latency in your own browser while driving. On Chrome, 1,000 consecutive JS Micro-VM + WASM MBA calls finish in roughly 8 to 45 milliseconds (~0.008 to 0.046 ms per call) with zero dropped frames.

    It has been revealed that if you are into reverse engineering, you can also download the 100% offline bundle (vault-engine.js, enclave.wasm, and challenge-cli.js) straight from the challenge page (or on Crackmes.one once approved). Every lock is deterministically solvable with zero brute-forcing, and solving all three keys decrypts a hidden flag and a note from our team.

    Next.js 16 Turbopack or any static dist/ folder (Post-Build CLI):.

    If you test it on your own project or try reversing SYFER-DRIFT, drop your burst benchmark numbers or feedback in the comments. Always happy to hear where real reverse engineers and builders find rough edges!

    วันที่ 24 พฤศจิกายน (ค.ศ. 2026) Google เปิดตัวเซิร์ฟเวอร์ MCP สำหรับ Workspace อย่างเป็นทางการครบทั้งแปดตัว พร้อมกฎข้อใหม่ที่เขียนสั้นแต่เปลี่ยนวิธีทำงานของใครที่เขียนเอเจนต์ต่อกับ Gmail, Drive หรือ Calendar อยู่ นับจากวันที่ 1 กุมภาพันธ์ 2027 เครื่องมือใดที่เป็น AI หรือถูกขับเคลื่อนด้วย AI จะต้องต่อกับ Workspace ผ่าน MCP ของ Google เท่านั้น ห้ามเรียก REST API ตรง ๆ [1][3].

    ปัญหาอยู่ตรงที่เมื่อเปิดเซิร์ฟเวอร์ Gmail ดูจริง ๆ จะพบว่ามันค้นเมลได้ อ่านเมลได้ สร้างฉบับร่างได้ แต่ส่งเมลไม่ได้ [4].

    ข้อความบังคับอยู่ในเอกสารเพิ่มเติมชื่อ Workspace AI Tools Addendum ที่แนบกับข้อตกลงใช้บริการ ผมอ่านจากตัวเอกสารจริง ข้อแรกระบุตรง ๆ ว่าเครื่องมือเข้าถึง Workspace ต้องใช้ MCP ของ Google ในกรณีที่เครื่องมือนั้นเป็น AI Agent, เป็น AI Harness หรือถูกขับเคลื่อนด้วยโมเดล AI หรือบริการที่ใช้โมเดล AI [2].

    ข้อถัดไปห้ามพรางตัวเอเจนต์ให้พ้นการจำแนก เมื่อทำผิด Google สามารถตัดสิทธิ์การเข้าถึงหรือระงับบัญชีได้ [2].

    ข้อบังคับเรื่อง MCP ครอบเฉพาะเครื่องมือ AI ในบันทึกประจำรุ่นเดือนตุลาคม Google เขียนเองว่าแอปที่ไม่ใช่เอเจนต์ AI เช่นโปรแกรมที่เรียก REST API เท่านั้น ไม่ได้รับผลกระทบจากการเปลี่ยนแปลงเรื่องการจำแนก OAuth client ครั้งนี้ [3].

    ส่วนการจัดชั้นโควตาใหม่เป็นอีกเรื่องหนึ่ง ใช้กับ API ของ Workspace โดยรวม ไม่ใช่เฉพาะเอเจนต์ [1].

    คู่มือทางการของเซิร์ฟเวอร์ Gmailระบุว่ามีเครื่องมือให้ใช้สิบตัว แบ่งเป็นสามกลุ่มงาน [4].

    ทว่าคู่มือไม่ใช่ขอบเขตทั้งหมด หน้าโควตาทางการของ Google ซึ่งอัปเดตล่าสุด 24 พฤศจิกายน 2026 วันเดียวกับที่เปิดใช้งาน ขึ้นทะเบียนเครื่องมือของ Gmail ไว้ 31 ตัว โดยแปดตัวมีดอกจันกำกับว่าต้องมีสิทธิ์พันธมิตร [7] เหลือเครื่องมือสาธารณะ 23 ตัว รวมถึงการย้ายข้อความลงถังขยะและสแปมที่คู่มือไม่ได้ระบุว่ามีให้ใช้ ตัวเลข 23 ตรงกับผลยิง tools/list ในรายงานของ [6] และชุดงานที่ [5] ระบุว่าเปิดให้สาธารณะก็ตรงกัน.

    การส่งเมล ตอบกลับ ส่งต่อ และการแก้ไขฉบับร่างที่สร้างไว้แล้ว ไม่ปรากฏในเครื่องมือสาธารณะทั้งชุด เครื่องมือเหล่านี้มีอยู่จริงบนเซิร์ฟเวอร์เดียวกัน แต่ถูกกักไว้ให้เฉพาะพันธมิตรที่ได้รับอนุมัติ สองรายงานสื่อที่ตรวจแยกกันยืนยันตรงกันว่าหน้าโควตาของ Google ระบุว่าเครื่องมือกลุ่มนี้ต้องมีสิทธิ์พันธมิตรและยังไม่เปิดทั่วไป [5][6].

    ผลที่ตามมาคือลำดับงานที่พังกลางทาง ลองนึกภาพสถานการณ์นี้ คุณพิมพ์สั่งตัวช่วยว่า ร่างอีเมลตอบลูกค้าเรื่องงบประมาณ เอเจนต์ค้นเมลเจอ ร่างให้เรียบร้อย คุณอ่านแล้วคอมเมนต์ว่าเพิ่มส่วนลดและเปลี่ยนโทนให้ทางการขึ้น.

    จังหวะนี้พังทันที เพราะการแก้ฉบับร่างเดิมไม่ใช่เครื่องมือสาธารณะ เอเจนต์มีทางเดียวคือสร้างร่างใหม่อีกฉบับแล้วทิ้งอันเก่าไว้ให้คุณลบเอง.

    ฝั่ง Drive ก็เจอแบบเดียวกันในระดับเบากว่า เอเจนต์สร้างรายงานเสร็จแต่ย้ายเข้าโฟลเดอร์ที่ถูกต้องหรือแชร์ให้ทีมเองไม่ได้ [5].

    รายละเอียดเชิงเทคนิคสำหรับคนจะลอง: เซิร์ฟเวอร์แต่ละตัวอยู่ที่โดเมนของตัวเอง เช่น gmailmcp.googleapis.com โดยมีปลายทางหลัก /mcp/v1 และปลายทาง /mcp/v1self สำหรับโปรแกรมที่ไม่รองรับการยืนยันผ่านแบบฟอร์ม สิทธิ์ที่ขอคือชุดเดียวกับ REST เช่น gmail.readonly กับ gmail.compose [4].

    อีกข้อในเอกสารเพิ่มเติมที่คนเขียนเอเจนต์จะรู้สึกถึงที่สุดคือการห้ามเก็บข้อมูลจำพวก Google Technical Information เกิน 30 วัน คำนิยามของข้อมูลกลุ่มนี้ครอบคลุมถึง vector embeddings, ดัชนีความจำ โปรไฟล์ผู้ใช้ และผังความสัมพันธ์ในองค์กรที่สร้างจากข้อมูล Workspace โดยที่ตัวข้อมูลของผู้ใช้เช่นเนื้อความอีเมลไม่ได้ถูกลบตามกฎ 30 วันนี้ ส่วนที่ห้ามเก็บคือผลสังเคราะห์ที่เอเจนต์สร้างขึ้นจากการใช้งาน [2].

    แปลง่าย ๆ ว่าตัวช่วยที่สร้างความจำระยะยาวจากกล่องจดหมายเพื่อตอบคำถามเรื่องสัญญาปีที่แล้ว จะต้องสร้างดัชนีใหม่ทุกเดือนหรือปล่อยความสามารถนี้ไป.

    พร้อมกันนั้นยังห้ามใช้ข้อมูลไปเทรนโมเดลหรือสร้างผลิตภัณฑ์ที่แข่งกับ Workspace และเมื่อผู้ใช้ถอดเอเจนต์ออก ข้อมูลที่เก็บไว้ต้องถูกลบทิ้งด้วย [2].

    ระดับพื้นฐานฟรี ได้ 5,000 คำขอต่อวันต่อโปรเจกต์ต่อผลิตภัณฑ์ แต่คำขอหนึ่งครั้งไม่เท่ากันเสมอไป เครื่องมือที่ต้องเรียก API หลายชั้นเบื้องหลังจะถูกนับเป็นหลายคำขอ [3].

    โควตานี้แชร์กันทั้งโปรเจกต์ ผลิตภัณฑ์เล็กที่มีผู้ใช้หลายคนจะชนเพดานเร็วกว่าที่คิด ตัวอย่างจากรายงานของสื่อเทคโนโลยีคือเครื่องมือค้นเมลหนึ่งครั้งถูกนับเป็นสิบคำขอ เอเจนต์ที่ทำแต่การค้นเมลจะได้ราวห้าร้อยครั้งต่อวันรวมทุกผู้ใช้ [5].

    ระดับ Scaled สำหรับงานหนักเริ่มคิดเงินวันที่ 1 เมษายน 2027 โดยหน้าทางการสองหน้าระบุต่างกันเอง หนึ่งบอกคิดตั้งแต่คำขอแรกของ MCP อีกหน้าบอกคิดเฉพาะส่วนที่เกินโควตาฟรีต่อวัน ส่วนโควตาฟรีขนาดใหญ่ของ REST ยังอยู่กับการเรียกแบบเดิม ซึ่งอ่านได้ว่าเป็นโครงสร้างราคาที่ผลักให้เอเจนต์ต้องอยู่บนเส้นทางของ Google [1][3][5].

    ความเห็นส่วนตัว: ผมอ่านแล้วเห็นสองด้านชัดทั้งคู่ ด้านความปลอดภัย เหตุผลของ Google มีน้ำหนักจริง เพราะโทเคนที่ได้รับมาไม่ได้แปลว่าเจตนาของคน อีเมลฉบับหนึ่งที่เขียนว่าให้ส่งอีเมลสิบฉบับข้างหน้าไปที่อยู่นี้ คือความเสี่ยงโจมตีแบบพรอมต์อินเจกชันที่มีอยู่จริง การบังคับให้ทุกเอเจนต์เดินผ่านประตูบานเดียวที่ผู้ดูแลองค์กรตั้งกฎยืนยันจากมนุษย์และบันทึกการใช้งานไว้ได้ ทำให้ผู้ดูแลคุมได้จริง แต่อีกด้านคือของที่ปิดไว้ให้เฉพาะพันธมิตร คนทำผลิตภัณฑ์อิสระจะได้เล่นในสนามที่ตัดสิทธิ์เฉพาะกิจ และเส้นทางเดิมที่เคยเปิดกว้างก็ถูกปิดลงพร้อมกัน สำหรับทีมไทยที่ทำตัวช่วยอีเมลหรือระบบออโตเมชัน AI ต่อ Workspace ผมว่าอย่ารอถึงมกราคม ประเมินว่าผลิตภัณฑ์ตัวเองอยู่ด้านไหนของกฎเสียตั้งแต่ตอนนี้ครับ.

    ถ้าคุณกำลังย้ายเอเจนต์ไป MCP อยู่และเจอปัญหาอะไร คอมเมนต์เล่าไว้ได้ครับ และถ้าบทนี้ช่วยได้ แชร์ให้ทีมที่ทำงานกับ Workspace ด้วยก็จะดีมาก.

    fm-cli is in the official Omarchy package repo

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (207 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • fm-cli, my little terminal client for Fastmail, is now an optional package in the official Omarchy repo.
    • Industry observers note that on Omarchy, open the menu with Super + Space, choose Install > Package, and type fm-cli.
    • Then sign in with fm-cli auth login, which opens Fastmail's consent page in your browser.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I have been waiting on this one. fm-cli, my little terminal client for Fastmail, is now an optional package in the official Omarchy repo. It is not on the default install, which is fine: it is there if you want it, and it is not in anyone's way if you don't.

    Industry observers note that on Omarchy, open the menu with Super + Space, choose Install > Package, and type fm-cli. Or, from a terminal:.

    Then sign in with fm-cli auth login, which opens Fastmail's consent page in your browser. That is it.

    fm-cli is a small Go client for Fastmail's JMAP API. It gives you a full-screen mail app in the terminal, commands that print JSON, a live watch over Fastmail's push connection, and offline reading and drafting. It is also the engine behind the Fastmail plugin for Omarchy.

    Industry observers note that the package that landed today is 0.3.3. Newer releases, up to 0.3.6, are on GitHub and still installable with mise if you want the latest. I'll work on getting the official package caught up.

    If you are not on Omarchy, the usual options are still there: mise, autonomix-cli, and the .deb, .rpm and tarball releases.

    Originally posted on blog.ninepointlabs.com.
